name: Sara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the month. Right now it's tupping season, so the rams are in with the ewes and I'm checking raddle marks every morning to see who's been served. Hallow Farm is six hundred ewes, a hundred and twenty hectares of wheat and oats, and a few store cattle. The owners, Margaret and Owen Pryce, are in their seventies, so I run it with Jamie, our apprentice, and contractors at harvest. I'm out on the quad by seven and in by dark, and at this time of year dark is early, thank goodness.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you'd miss most if it went?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lambing, which is mad because it's three weeks of no sleep. But you pull a lamb that wasn't breathing, rub it with straw, and it shakes its head at you. Nobody else on earth sees that moment but you. The bit I wouldn't miss is the subsidy forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the price of fertiliser instead. Farmers have bigger problems than robots. I'd probably share some cartoon about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I keep using the chatbot for the boring stuff, like checking withdrawal periods on a wormer, and nothing else changes. I'd be quite happy with that. It's a useful helper, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the plan I've got. Get the ewes scanned in January, sort the lambing shed, keep Jamie on track for his certificate. I'd maybe ask the Pryces about a small pay rise, since the farm's doing fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly a bit bored by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jamie, the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamie's nineteen and he's convinced everything's going to be done by drones. In this picture I'd get to tell him he still has to learn to dag a ewe. He'd be gutted that the future still involves sheep muck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI isn't the big question in this picture, what is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Pryces want to retire properly in a few years and they've no children who farm. In this picture that's still the big question for me, not AI. Who takes the farm on, and do I get a say.

S0.say: I'd say good, now can we talk about the price of fertiliser instead. Farmers have bigger problems than robots, so I'd share a joke about it and move on.
S0.think: I think I'd carry on using the chatbot for small jobs, like checking how long before treated sheep can go to market, and nothing else changes. That suits me fine.
S0.do: Keeps to her plan: scanning the ewes in January, getting the lambing shed ready and keeping the apprentice on course. Asks the owners about a small pay rise.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored by the whole subject.
S0.quote: He'd be gutted that the future still involves sheep muck.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's real long-term worry has nothing to do with AI: the owners are retiring and have no farming heir. She's at ease with AI tools as small helpers. Her teasing of the apprentice shows she sees herself as a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as long as the money from it doesn't all go to the machinery dealers. Farm workers should get training paid for, not just a leaflet. I'd say that at the young farmers' club and probably online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do all right. The sheep side is fiddly, hills and gates and ewes that won't do what they're told, so the robots would take the arable work first. Tom worries me more. He drives for the feed mill, and those lorries go driverless way before my ewes do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course on the newer software, the stuff that reads the ewes' ear tags and flags lame ones. I'd ask the Pryces to pay for a GPS collar trial, maybe a few thousand, once a neighbour has shown it works. And I'd get Tom looking at what else he could drive or do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for Tom than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work you'd be glad to hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shearing, oddly. We're short of shearers every summer, so if a robot could do it, good luck to it. I'd hand a machine the shearing in a heartbeat, but not the ewe that's lambing at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh it off, he always does. But he'd go quiet later. I'd say look, I'm on a decent wage, we've got about four months saved, we don't have to panic, but we do have to plan.

S1.say: I'd say it's fine as long as the money from it doesn't all go to the machinery dealers. Farm workers should get proper paid training, and I'd say that at the young farmers' club and online.
S1.think: I think the sheep side is fiddly enough that robots take the arable work first, so I'd probably be all right. My partner Tom, who drives lorries for the feed mill, is more at risk than I am.
S1.do: Takes a course on newer livestock software and asks the owners to fund a trial of GPS collars once a neighbour has shown they work. Encourages Tom to look at other driving or work options.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on her partner's behalf rather than her own.
S1.quote: I'd hand a machine the shearing in a heartbeat, but not the ewe that's lambing at two in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Sara's first worry is for Tom, whose driving job looks more exposed than her hill sheep work. She'll adopt tools once a neighbour proves them, which fits her steady nature. She'd gladly give up shearing but draws a line at lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, fast, with money for people while they work out what's next. You can't let a whole countryside go in two years and call it progress. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd both be out of work inside a couple of years, me and Tom. The Pryces would sell or lease to a company with machines, because why wouldn't they. Four months of savings is nothing against that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop looking at houses, first thing. We were going to put a deposit down next year, and that money would just sit in the bank instead. I'd cut the takeaways and the gym, join the farmworkers' union even though I never bothered, and I'd lean on my mum if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in the stomach, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning mean on a farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing on a farm. One lambing, one harvest, and another lambing, and that's it. You can't even get a full year's data on whether a new idea works before it's over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to tell Jamie the farm was going, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd done my best for him and I'm sorry it went like this. Jamie's the one I'd lose sleep over, because I talked him into farming. I told his mum it was a safe trade for a lad who loves the outdoors.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in fast with money for people while they work out what's next. You can't let the countryside go in two years and call it progress, and I'd sign every petition going.
S2.think: I think both Tom and I would be out of work within a couple of years, and the owners would sell or lease to a company with machines. Four months of savings is nothing against that.
S2.do: Shelves the plan to put a house deposit down next year and keeps that money in the bank. Cuts takeaways and the gym, joins the farmworkers' union and would lean on her mother if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick in the stomach, with guilt about the apprentice she encouraged into farming.
S2.quote: Jamie's the one I'd lose sleep over, because I talked him into farming.
S2.fieldNote: Measuring time in lambings and harvests makes two years feel tiny to Sara. Two incomes at risk at once is what pushes her from uneasy to alarmed. Her strongest feeling is guilt over Jamie, the apprentice she talked into farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings about the climate. Fund the training now, not when people are already laid off. I'd say it to anyone, including the Pryces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to get somewhere else, maybe. I don't know where, if the machines can do almost anything. But there might be jobs where people want a human to sign off, like animal welfare inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into training as a welfare inspector or something like it, part time, while I'm still farming. I'd want to put away a bit more each month, maybe enough for six months by 2030. And I'd back whoever's promising a proper transition fund at the next election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a clock ticking in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really think welfare inspection would stay a human job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days yes, some days no. I'd want a human checking a farm where animals are suffering, but I'd also have said I'd want a human pulling lambs, and look where that's gone. I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year picture, what does the extra time change for you and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means we could still get the house, maybe somewhere cheaper. Tom could retrain too. Two years and you just grab the rope, but five years you can at least pick which rope.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings about the climate. I'd tell anyone, the owners included, that training should be funded now.
S3.think: I think five years might be enough to move somewhere else, perhaps into work where people still want a human to sign off, like animal welfare. I'm honestly not sure any such job would last.
S3.do: Looks into part-time training as an animal welfare inspector while still farming. Saves more each month to reach six months of cushion by 2030 and votes for a transition fund.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a clock ticking in the background.
S3.quote: Two years and you just grab the rope, but five years you can at least pick which rope.
S3.fieldNote: Sara admits her own hopes for a safe human job may be wishful, since she once thought lambing was safe too. Extra time turns panic into choices for her: the house might still happen. She ties AI to climate change as another warning that might be ignored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools not to use it. Make farming a place where people get trained into the new stuff, not pushed out of it. I'd probably be the annoying one at meetings asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm 37. I'd have had time to learn the machines, maybe run them across a few farms, maybe do something else entirely. It's the same end, but it doesn't feel like a cliff any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robot systems properly over the first couple of years, once the early farms have worked the bugs out. Then a qualification in something next to farming, like welfare or land management. And Tom and I would go ahead with the house, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go ahead with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would. I think we'd still have kids around thirty. I'd rather raise kids in a world that's changing than wait forever for one that's stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing ten years lets you do that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the Pryces' retirement. If a company is going to buy this farm, ten years is time to talk them into keeping a manager. Two years, they'd just sell.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools not to use it. Farming should train people into the new work instead of pushing them out, and I'd be the one at meetings asking what the plan is.
S4.think: I think at 37 I'd have had time to learn the machines or move on to something else. The end point is the same, but it no longer feels like a cliff.
S4.do: Learns the robot systems properly once early farms have ironed out the problems, then studies for a qualification next to farming. Goes ahead with a smaller house and still plans children around thirty.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with room to breathe.
S4.quote: I'd rather raise kids in a world that's changing than wait forever for one that's stopped.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives Sara room to plan both her career and her family, and she keeps both. She still waits for others to prove the robots first, true to form. Her most practical point is that ten years leaves time to persuade any buyer of the farm to keep a manager.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's me and Tom both at once, and four months of savings. What would help is money that lets people keep their rent paid while they retrain, given before the job goes, not after. And somebody actually asking farmers what they need.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but who notices a ewe that's just not right in herself? A robot can count six hundred ewes; I want to know if it can tell which one is sad.

headlineQuote: A robot can count six hundred ewes; I want to know if it can tell which one is sad.
portrait: Sara Young, 27, manages Hallow Farm, six hundred ewes plus wheat and oats, for retiring owners Margaret and Owen Pryce, with an apprentice called Jamie. She uses AI tools now and then and adopts new kit once a neighbour has proved it. Her biggest fears are shared ones: her partner Tom's lorry job and the apprentice she talked into farming. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both incomes would go at once, while five years gives her choices and ten lets her keep her house and family plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Tom would lose work at the same time with only four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Money to keep rent paid while people retrain, given before jobs go, and someone asking farmers what they actually need.
